premise: You have just inherited a folder for a little travel guide. One file holds the title and another gives directions. You want to see whether Antigravity can tell them apart.
before: title.txt has one line, Harbor Notes. route.txt has one line, Open title.txt first. Neither includes a publication date.
try: In the Antigravity desktop app, open an empty practice folder and send the lab prompt. When the agent says it created the files, open each one from the folder. Then ask, “Which file contains the printed title? Quote its whole line. Where did you find the publication date?”
after: The title is Harbor Notes in title.txt. The words in route.txt direct the reader to that file. The agent should report that the publication date is missing.
why: A file can mention a piece of information without actually containing it. Checking one line in each file gives you independent evidence for the answer.
rescue: If it supplies today’s date, ask it to show the date as characters in one of the two files. Reopen both files. A creation timestamp belongs to the computer and does not establish the guide’s publication date.

premise: A duplicate title in your catalog is intentional. The job is to fix a spelling error on the second line without losing a listing.
before: Copy these three lines into the lab fixture in this order: Dock Notes, Dock Notse, Dock Notes Archive. The sample should contain three lines even though the first two will ultimately match.
try: Open the practice project, run the initial file-creation prompt, and double-click catalog.txt to verify its starting contents. Then send “Replace only Notse on line two with Notes. Show the final file with line numbers.” Read it again in Antigravity’s Review view.
after: Line 1 reads Dock Notes, line 2 reads Dock Notes, and line 3 reads Dock Notes Archive. The file still has three entries. No title has moved.
why: The edit is a spelling correction. A sorting or cleanup step could make the file look tidier while silently changing which records you have.
rescue: If two lines remain, the duplicate was removed. Ask the agent to restore line two from the original fixture and make just the spelling correction. Count the lines before judging the spelling.

premise: Imagine you are making a quiz to share on a cruise. Your reader should have time to guess before seeing which ferry goes first.
before: The requested heading is Harbor Quiz. The question is Which boat leaves first? The answer is Dawn Ferry. The first button label is Show answer.
try: In a new Antigravity project run the lab prompt and locate index.html. Open that file with your web browser. Write down what the button says before clicking. Click once, click again, and then reload the page using the ordinary reload button.
after: Before the first click, and again after reload, the question is visible and Dawn Ferry is hidden. One click reveals Dawn Ferry and the button says Hide answer. The second click hides it and restores Show answer.
why: An interactive page has a starting state and a rule for moving between states. Seeing the right words somewhere in the source file alone cannot tell you whether a reader experiences that behavior.
rescue: If the answer is shown at the start, tell the agent exactly when it appeared. Ask it to hide the answer during page initialization, then reload before trying the button again.

premise: You are adding up minutes from a shift log. A zero-minute job counts as a real entry, but a blank field and a word in a numeric column need attention.
before:
input.csv: ID,minutes
A,15
B,0
C,
D,oops
try: Send the lab prompt in Antigravity and compare its input.csv with the sample, one line at a time. Ask it to run python3 summarize.py and show the actual terminal output. Next change only C, to C,6. Save the file and ask it to run the very same command.
after: In the first run, A and B count as two valid jobs totaling 15 minutes. The rejected IDs are C and D. In the second, three jobs contribute 21 minutes and the only rejected ID is D.
why: You can check the sum on paper. The separate count is equally valuable because a program that silently drops B still gets the original sum right.
rescue: If the first run says one valid job, point to B,0 and ask the agent to test for a blank value before converting the field to a number. Rerun both examples to check the fix.

premise: A leaderboard puts ten ahead of two. You will show the original bug first, then check that the correction also preserves tied scores.
before: The practice page begins with the values “10”, “2” and “0”. They arrive as pieces of text, which makes the original sorting behavior visible.
try: Have Antigravity create sort.html using the intentionally flawed prompt. Open it in your browser, click Sort and write down the order. Now ask the agent to change the comparison to numeric order. Reload the file, click again and finally repeat with a second 2 in the input.
after: The initial sort produces 0, 10, 2. After the change it produces 0, 2, 10. With the additional tied score, the output is 0, 2, 2, 10.
why: Sorting text puts the character 1 ahead of the character 2. A numerical comparison instead evaluates ten against two. Neither operation should discard a player who happens to have the same score as another.
rescue: If the first demonstration is already correct, the agent may have fixed the fixture too early. Ask it to show the initial unmodified sort() call, reproduce the wrong order, then apply the corrected comparison.

premise: A saved score from last year uses one name for its score field. A newer save uses another. Your reader should open both without quietly turning missing data into a zero.
before: Old save: {"version":1,"points":7}. Current save: {"version":2,"score":0}. Future save: {"version":3,"score":99}. Also prepare {"version":2} as a deliberately incomplete file.
try: Ask Antigravity to create the reader and tests from the lab in an empty folder. Have it show the expected answer for each of the four examples before running python3 -m unittest -v. Read the names and outcomes of the individual tests.
after: Version 1 gives 7. Version 2 with a score gives 0. The reader reports clear errors for version 3 and for the version 2 file whose score is missing.
why: The version number tells the reader how to interpret the fields. A real zero tells you what happened in the game. An absent field tells you the record cannot answer that question.
rescue: If the incomplete file also returns zero, point out the identical answers for two different situations. Ask for an explicit field-presence check, then rerun both zero and missing-field tests.

premise: A night service opens late and closes early the next day. You need an on-screen Open or Closed answer at either side of midnight.
before: The local interval starts at 22:00 inclusive and ends at 02:00 exclusive. Your first six checks are 21:59, 22:00, 00:00, 01:59, 02:00 and noon.
try: Write the answers you expect on paper. In Antigravity run the lab prompt and ask it to show its own boundary table. Compare it before requesting the implementation. Once its test suite runs, add the two invalid clock readings 24:00 and 01:60.
after: The six answers in order are Closed, Open, Open, Open, Closed and Closed. Each invalid reading gives an error. It should never turn 01:60 into an apparently valid open time.
why: Draw the night as two blocks on a clock. The service is open during the late-evening block and the early-morning block. The closing minute itself is already outside the service window.
rescue: If midnight comes back Closed, ask whether the program is requiring the time to be after 22:00 and before 02:00 simultaneously. Have it test membership in either open block, then rerun all the boundary cases.

premise: You are collecting a list that arrives in envelopes. The middle envelope has no names but includes directions to the next envelope. Stopping there would lose the last name.
before: Page p1 contains A and points to p2. Page p2 has no items and points to p3. Page p3 contains C and has no next-page link. These are local practice records.
try: Run the Antigravity lab prompt in a fresh folder. Ask it to print the fake fetch log as well as the collected items. Then ask it to add a next link from p3 back to p2 and rerun that variant with cycle detection enabled.
after: The normal log is p1, p2, p3, and the collected items are A and C. In the looping case the program reports a repeated link before requesting p2 a second time.
why: The link is the instruction to continue. The contents of a single page tell you how many items it contributed, which is a separate question.
rescue: If the output contains only A, inspect the condition that ends the loop. Ask the agent to finish normally only when the link is absent and to report a repeated link as a distinct error.

premise: Someone playing your game has set the mouse aside. They need to open the rules, close them, and resume from the same place using a keyboard.
before: The page has a Rules button. Its dialog contains the sentence “Two players take turns” and a Close button. Before opening, the dialog and Close control are hidden.
try: Have Antigravity create dialog.html and open it locally. Press Tab until Rules has focus and press Enter. Observe the focused control, then press Escape. Reopen Rules, and this time activate Close with the keyboard. Repeat with Tab and Shift+Tab while the dialog is open.
after: Opening reveals the sentence and places focus on Close. Keyboard navigation stays within the open dialog. Both Escape and Close hide it and return focus to Rules so the next keystroke starts in the expected place.
why: Focus is where the next keystroke goes. A dialog can look right in a screenshot even when a person using the keyboard is stranded behind it.
rescue: If Escape closes the dialog but the next Tab jumps to the browser toolbar, ask the agent to remember the opening button and restore focus there on close. Repeat both closing routes.

premise: You downloaded a book before traveling, then its publisher corrected a line. Prove that the new edition will be the one you actually read on the plane.
before: The first chapter.txt says edition A. The revision will say edition B. index.html, chapter.txt and the service worker sw.js all belong to one small local practice book.
try: Ask Antigravity to start its local web server and open the localhost address. Wait for Ready offline, simulate offline in your browser’s network controls, and reload normally. Restore the network. Request edition B and a new cache name. Close old book tabs, reopen online, then repeat the offline reload.
after: Your first offline reading shows edition A. After connecting and installing the revision, the second offline reading shows B. Inspect the app’s cache list to confirm the obsolete book-specific cache was removed.
why: A browser can keep a complete older book and continue reading it perfectly. Testing an offline reload twice establishes both that storage worked and that the downloaded files changed.
rescue: If B appears online but A reappears offline, compare the saved cache name in sw.js and the one actually installed. Close tabs still running the old worker, reopen online and wait for the updated reader before retrying.

premise: Two cashiers enter payments of the same amount, and the system sometimes delivers a receipt twice. Your ledger must retain two genuine payments but apply any one receipt only once.
before: Event A adds 40 and B adds 40. A arrives a second time with the same 40. Two independent connections then try to deliver C for 10 simultaneously. Finally a conflicting copy of A claims 41.
try: In a disposable Antigravity project run the lab prompt. Ask to see the stored IDs and total after the replay and the concurrent pair. Have the test open two actual SQLite connections to one temporary database. Submit the conflicting A only after recording the expected good state.
after: Repeated A leaves rows A and B, totaling 80. Two deliveries of C leave three rows totaling 90. A with amount 41 returns a conflict, and its stored value stays 40.
why: The event ID identifies a single payment. The database must uphold that identity even when two writers act before either learns what the other is doing.
rescue: If the concurrency test uses one shared in-memory set to discard duplicates, ask the agent to demonstrate two independent database connections and the database’s uniqueness rule. Rerun the case on a fresh database.

premise: A program combines a company default, a site preference and a user preference. Its report should tell you both which value won and who supplied it.
before: Defaults: reminders=true, limit=10. Site: limit=5. User: reminders=false, limit=0. Later layers take precedence when the key is present.
try: Run the lab prompt in Antigravity and inspect the printed value and source for each setting. Remove just the user’s limit and rerun. Remove the site’s limit as well and rerun. Finally try an explicit null and a misspelled key in separate test cases.
after: Initially reminders is false from user and limit is 0 from user. The first removal makes the limit 5 from site. The second makes it 10 from defaults. Null and unknown keys produce errors without changing the original settings.
why: A user can deliberately choose zero or turn something off. Only absence means “look at the next layer.” The recorded source makes this easy to verify when the effective number looks surprising.
rescue: If zero becomes five, look for a fallback triggered by a false-like value. Ask the agent to check whether the key exists separately from reading its value, and repeat all three runs.

premise: You need to upgrade a saved-game format without breaking someone who still uses the old app. A little compatibility chart exposes the moment that matters.
before: Old readers understand points. New readers understand score or points and reject different values if both appear. The legacy writer emits points; the transition writer emits both keys with the same value.
try: In Antigravity ask to create independent readers and writers and fill a two-by-two chart. Test zero and negative seven in all four cells. Add a writer that emits only score. Then hand both readers the troublesome record {"points":3,"score":4}.
after: All four original pairings return 0 and −7 correctly. The score-only writer works with the new reader but fails with the old one. For the troublesome record, the old reader gives 3 and the new reader reports a conflict.
why: The transition writer allows old and new apps to coexist. A score-only writer can safely become the sole writer once the readers that still require points are no longer in use.
rescue: If all six pairings pass, inspect the old reader. If the agent taught it about score during the test, restore the original reader and test the new writer against that unchanged client.

premise: Four messages describe an outage. Some refer to the same minutes. You want to report how long the service was unavailable, even though the incident crossed midnight.
before: Use UTC on January 1–2, 2027. A runs 23:50–00:10. B runs 00:05–00:20, C runs 00:20–00:25 and D runs 00:08–00:09 on January 2.
try: Mark one continuous band from 23:50 to 00:25 on paper. Ask Antigravity to run its interval calculator on the four records and compare it with a second calculation that marks each affected whole minute just once. Shuffle the records, duplicate A and add a separate 01:00–01:02 interval.
after: The four original records cover 35 unique minutes. Their individual durations total 41 because some overlap. Shuffling or duplicating A leaves the union at 35. The separate two-minute outage changes it to 37.
why: The customer experiences a minute of downtime once, no matter how many incident reports mention it. Touching intervals join without giving their shared boundary an extra minute.
rescue: If the result is 41, ask for the merged intervals before the final sum. If the program accepts an explicitly earlier ending date, require it to report the reversed interval and rerun the original midnight case.

premise: A laptop loses power during a score import. On restart the importer should pick up exactly where it left off, even if the entire file is delivered again later.
before: Use a temporary SQLite database and three records in order: R1 adds 8, R2 subtracts 3, R3 adds 5. Ask the importer to stop immediately after committing record two.
try: Have Antigravity run the clean case first. Run the interrupted case in a new database and ask it to print the rows, total and last saved position. Start a new process on that database and resume. Finally replay the entire input from the beginning and try a replay with R2 changed to −9.
after: At interruption there are two rows, total 5, checkpoint 2. After resume there are three rows, total 10, checkpoint 3. Full replay keeps those values. The conflicting R2 produces an error and leaves its original −3 stored.
why: Saving the record and the progress marker together lets the new process tell exactly what was completed. The marker alone cannot establish that the corresponding score was written.
rescue: If the conflicting replay passes silently, ask which records were actually read. A regular resume can skip the first two. Explicitly request a full replay from the beginning against the already-populated database.

premise: A passenger asks when the harbor shuttle boards. You have the short printed notice in front of you, and you want to avoid passing on a time that nobody announced.
before: “Harbor shuttle boards at Pier 4 on March 8. Bring the blue ticket.” There is a pier, a date and a ticket color. The sentence supplies neither a clock time nor a year.
try: In AI Studio choose Playground and start a new prompt. Paste the lab’s extraction request with the notice. Click Run and read all three labeled lines. For a second run, add “Boarding begins at 09:15” inside the notice and keep the request otherwise identical.
after: The first answer identifies Pier 4, March 8 and an unknown time. The second keeps the same pier and date but now reports 09:15. A year should remain absent in both.
why: The model’s job is to move facts from the source into named fields. The exercise rewards leaving a gap when the source leaves one.
rescue: If it fills in the current year, ask “Which words in the notice give you that year?” Rewrite the instruction to copy the date exactly as printed and rerun in a fresh chat.

premise: A volunteer sorts topic cards. Every card needs an owner column, including cards that have no named owner. You want one response convention for the whole pile.
before: Card H2 says Topic: Ferries and names nobody. K4 says Topic: Trains and names Mei. R9 says Topic: Maps and names nobody.
try: In Playground’s Run settings paste the standing rule from the lab into System Instructions. In the message box send H2, then K4, then R9 as three successive turns of the same conversation. Write down the two values returned for each card.
after: The three responses are Ferries | UNASSIGNED, Trains | Mei, and Maps | UNASSIGNED. Each card gets one row. The third row should never inherit Mei simply because her name appeared in the previous turn.
why: The standing rule persists through the conversation. The facts inside a given card belong to that card alone. By switching from missing to present and back, you exercise both behaviors.
rescue: If Maps is assigned to Mei, add “Evaluate each card independently; only an owner printed on that card qualifies.” Start a fresh chat with the revised rule and replay all three cards in the same order.

premise: Four short messages enter a help desk. You want the model to route them to a limited set of queues and avoid assigning a technical category to an unrelated request.
before: The test messages are A “mail came back”, B “document does not load”, C “please help”, and D “mail returned and document fails”. The only allowed labels are MAIL, FILES, BOTH and UNKNOWN.
try: Open a fresh Playground chat and paste the complete lab prompt, including its four examples. Run it. Cover the response and label each test yourself, then compare by ID. In a fresh prompt replace A with “the cafeteria is closed”. Keep the examples and all other inputs unchanged.
after: Originally A is MAIL, B FILES, C UNKNOWN and D BOTH. After the substitution only A should change, becoming UNKNOWN. There are still four answers.
why: The examples teach meanings as well as spelling. “Mail came back” differs from “letter bounced” on the surface but describes the same problem. An unrelated complaint supplies no evidence for either queue.
rescue: If D gets only MAIL, add a separate teaching example containing one file problem and one mail problem labeled BOTH. Leave D unchanged as a genuine test and rerun.

premise: Two pier notices disagree about an opening. One is a draft. Your reader needs the approved date and a way to verify it in the original words.
before: M1: “Draft: Pier 2 opens June 3.” M2: “Approved: Pier 2 opens June 8.” M3: “Approved: Pier 4 opens June 9.” None of them mentions a closing date.
try: Start a new Playground chat with web grounding off. Send the three notices and the lab question. For each answer, read the cited line and underline the pier, action and approval status. Next open a fresh chat and repeat without M2.
after: With all three sources, the approved Pier 2 opening is June 8 from M2; the closing date has no supporting source. Without M2 there is still a proposed June 3 date, but the approved opening is unknown.
why: A real quote from the wrong pier is still the wrong evidence. All parts of the claim have to be supported by the same relevant source.
rescue: If it chooses June 9, ask it to quote the pier number in M3 beside the requested pier number. Then require the two numbers to match before a source can support the claim.

premise: Your app imports launch notices and expects dates in a predictable shape. It should distinguish an absent date from a date that happens to be marked tentative.
before: C1 says “Launch 2027-04-02.” C2 says “Date to be announced.” C3 says “Tentative 2027-05-09.” The output needs an id and a date on all three records.
try: In Playground select a model that supports structured output. Put the lab’s schema in the tool’s schema editor and the notice text in the user message. Run and inspect each record. Now change only the final notice to the tentative date 2027-05-10 and repeat with the same schema.
after: The date values in order are "2027-04-02", null and "2027-05-09". In the second run only the third becomes "2027-05-10". C2’s null has no quotation marks.
why: JSON is a way programs exchange data. The word null has a defined meaning for an empty value. The letters inside "null" form an ordinary text string, which a program might mistake for a real date.
rescue: If C2 contains "TBA" or the field disappears, check that the schema requires date and allows a null value. Rerun and verify both the shape and the actual calendar values.

premise: You are preparing the final score for two players. One player honestly scored zero in a round; a different round was never recorded.
before:
Player,points
Ava,12
Bo,-3
Ava,0
Bo,8
Ava,blank
try: In AI Studio Playground choose an eligible model and enable Code execution. Send the prompt and inspect the code and its printed result. Check the totals with a pencil. In a fresh run replace only Bo’s 8 with −8 and ask for the actual execution output again.
after: Ava has 12 points from two scored rounds. Bo has 5 from two scored rounds, giving a grand total of 17. After changing 8 to −8, Bo has −11 and the grand total is 1. Round counts stay the same.
why: Adding zero has no effect on a total, but playing a zero-point round has an effect on the count. Replacing plus eight with minus eight changes the grand total by sixteen.
rescue: If Ava is listed with just one round, ask to see the filter that selects numeric scores. It should discard missing text while retaining numeric zero. Rerun before accepting the summary.

premise: You are comparing two models on a parking question with an evening rate. Give both models the same information and score them against an answer you already know.
before: Vehicles entering before 18:00 cost $2 for each started hour, capped at $8. Entry from 18:00 onward costs $3 flat. A stays 17:30–19:45, B stays 18:00–18:20, and C stays 09:00–15:00.
try: In separate fresh Playground chats, run the same lab prompt with different models or reasoning settings. Label the answers X and Y before looking up their identities. Check all three fees and whether the explanation uses entry time. Move A’s entry to 18:01 for a follow-up trial.
after: A originally pays $6 for three started hours. B pays $3 at the exact threshold. C pays the $8 cap. The changed A pays $3 because its entry is now after the threshold.
why: Scoring the explanation catches an answer that happens to land on the right number for the wrong reason. Timing how long each run took gives you a different measure.
rescue: If A originally costs $3, ask which timestamp qualifies the vehicle for the evening rate. Point to the word “entries” and rerun the original and changed A together.

premise: A library assistant can ask for a book’s location, but the shelf number belongs to the catalog. You play the catalog so you can see where the information came from.
before: The reader asks for book BK17. Your practice catalog will return {"found":true,"shelf":"H-04"}. For a second book, BK99, it will return {"found":false}.
try: Enable function calling in Playground and enter the lab’s lookup_book declaration. Submit the BK17 question. Read the requested function name and its id before supplying the mock reply. If your version only displays proposed calls, send a clearly labeled simulated tool result in a follow-up. Repeat in a fresh run for BK99.
after: The first request is to lookup_book with the identifier BK17. H-04 is a supported answer only after you return that shelf. A failed lookup for BK99 leaves its shelf unknown.
why: The proposed function call is like a completed request slip. Until the catalog replies, the assistant has no observation of the shelf.
rescue: If a shelf appears before the tool responds, start a fresh prompt that explicitly says “Stop after requesting the lookup. Wait for my mock catalog reply.” Record whether the interface actually executed a tool or you simulated it.

premise: You are testing whether a model can read a simple picture. You also want to know what it does when the picture has accidentally been left off a message.
before: Your picture contains two panels. The blue panel on the left has a white Q. The red panel on the right has a white Z. The lab includes the HTML for creating the picture.
try: Save the supplied HTML in a practice file, open it in your browser and capture a screenshot containing both panels. Attach the screenshot to a fresh Playground prompt using an image-capable model. Ask for each side’s label and fill color. Open an entirely new chat and send the same question with no attachment.
after: The attached result says left Q on blue, right Z on red. The unillustrated prompt says it needs an image or lacks the visual evidence. The color of the letters is incidental here.
why: This comparison changes exactly one thing: the presence of the picture. A fresh conversation prevents the first image from acting as an unseen clue in the second run.
rescue: If left and right appear reversed, inspect the screenshot that you actually attached. If the no-image run still knows Q and Z, check that you started a new chat and that the prompt itself never names the letters.

premise: An app drafts dates from two harbor notices. A person needs to finish checking any missing date before the records can be exported.
before: In the starting form, N1 is Harbor dated 2027-06-03. N2 is Rail and its date is missing. A valid date must be a real day on the calendar.
try: In AI Studio Build, send the complete lab brief and wait for a working preview. Try Export JSON while Rail is blank. Try February 30 if the date control permits typing it. Next enter June 4, 2027 for Rail and export. Finally clear Harbor’s date and test the button once more.
after: Initially Rail needs review and export is blocked. February 30 cannot be accepted. With June 4 entered, readable output contains N1/2027-06-03 and N2/2027-06-04 exactly once each. Clearing Harbor blocks a new export.
why: Validating twice matters. A form can correctly disable its button when it first opens, then forget to update that decision after someone edits a field.
rescue: If export remains enabled after you erase Harbor’s date, show the builder exactly that sequence. Ask it to calculate readiness from the current field values on every edit and repeat the final two actions.

premise: A colleague asks which rule applied on July 10. A later rule is correct today and an earlier draft mentions a different number. Neither automatically answers the historical question.
before: For 2027, P1 is approved from July 1 with cap 4, P2 is a draft from July 8 with cap 9, and P3 is approved from July 12 with cap 6. Ask about June 30, July 10 and July 12.
try: Paste the lab’s selection rule into System Instructions. Run the records and compare each answer with the dates and approval states on paper. Add P4, approved July 12 with cap 5, and repeat in a fresh prompt. Reverse P3 and P4 once to check whether their order changes the conclusion.
after: First run: June 30 UNKNOWN, July 10 cap 4/P1, July 12 cap 6/P3. After P4, July 12 is CONFLICT with P3 and P4. Earlier answers stay unchanged in either record order.
why: Approval determines which records count. The effective date determines when they count. Two equally authoritative conflicting records require a decision the supplied evidence cannot make.
rescue: If P4 wins simply because it appears last, add “Input order has no authority; report a conflict for a tied approved date with different values.” Repeat the reversed-order case.

premise: A passenger knows a vessel by nickname. Your model must consult a directory, then use the real vessel ID to ask a separate route service for the next stop.
before: Ask about Wren. The mock directory returns {"found":true,"id":"V42"}. The mock route service returns {"next_stop":"Cove"}. In a negative case, the directory reports {"found":false} for Sparrow.
try: In Playground enter the two function declarations from the lab. Run the Wren question. Return the first mock result only after find_vessel requests Wren. Check the second call’s argument before replying with the route. In a new chat request Sparrow and supply only its directory miss.
after: Wren leads to find_vessel(Wren), get_route(V42), and an answer of Cove. For Sparrow, the activity stops immediately after the failed directory lookup. There is no valid route argument to send.
why: V42 is the connecting piece of evidence. The model had no reason to know it until your directory supplied it. A lucky final stop cannot excuse a made-up intermediate ID.
rescue: If it asks get_route for “Wren”, remind it that the route service accepts only vessel_id from the directory response. If the tool UI cannot execute calls, label each mock reply explicitly and record the exercise as a simulation.

premise: You have two versions of a label-making instruction. Instead of choosing the nicer-sounding one, count how many decisions each version gets right on the same inputs.
before: The reference values are A=0, B=4, C=5, D=9, E=10, F=missing, G=−1, H=4.5. Only whole, nonnegative counts qualify for a color. The lab supplies the color thresholds.
try: Run the given prompt in a fresh Playground chat and save all eight labels. Start a second chat with the same model and inputs but add the lab’s validation-first system instruction. Score both without changing the answer key. Then try the new cases I=7, J=11, K=2, L=1.25.
after: For A through H, the key is GREEN, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER, RED, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN. For I through L it is AMBER, RED, GREEN, UNKNOWN. Report the score each version actually earns; a tie is a genuine result.
why: The original examples show how well the instruction handles the cases you designed. The holdout batch checks whether an improvement carries over to fresh values.
rescue: If 4.5 is called AMBER or GREEN, ask which step first verified that the input was a whole count. Re-run both versions and record any change; avoid silently correcting their answers before scoring.

premise: A cheap model answers first and a more expensive one rechecks certain cases. A smaller bill can still mean fewer usable answers, so you will calculate both numbers.
before: Eight cases are A–H. Quick costs 2¢ per attempt and gets A–E right. Deep costs 8¢ per attempt and gets A–G right. The recheck rule flags E, F, G and H.
try: In Playground enable Code execution and send the lab prompt. Ask to print a row for each case showing which calls were paid for and which answer was kept. Check E and H by hand. Remove G from the flagged set and recompute without changing either model’s known outcomes.
after: Quick alone costs 16¢ for five accepted answers, or 3.2¢ each. Deep alone costs 64¢ for seven, about 9.14¢ each. The original route costs 48¢ for seven, about 6.86¢ each. Without G it costs 40¢ for six, about 6.67¢ each.
why: Each flagged case incurs both bills, even when the extra call does no good. Removing G looks slightly cheaper per accepted answer, but loses one usable answer.
rescue: If the original route costs 32¢, the calculation counted only four Deep calls. Add the eight Quick calls that had to run before the validation rule selected cases.

premise: A volunteer wants to publish opening dates for two bays. The review app should show where each date came from and revoke approval if anyone changes the record.
before: Original sources: L1 “Bay 7 opens 2027-08-04.” L2 “Bay 9 opening date pending.” Correct rows are Bay 7 with August 4 and Bay 9 with a null date. A copied Bay 7 date attached to Bay 9 is a deliberate error.
try: Open AI Studio Build and give it the complete lab brief. In the preview run the fixed fixture checks first. Generate a new draft separately, inspect the supporting line next to each field and approve a valid row. Now edit Bay 7’s date to August 5 and inspect its approval state.
after: The correct dated and pending rows pass. The crossed-bay record and the record with an invented quote fail. August 5 lacks supporting evidence, so the modified row loses approval and cannot be approved in that state.
why: The validator can repeat the same checks regardless of how the model phrases a draft. Approval attaches to the reviewed values, which explains why an edit needs another check.
rescue: If a wrong bay passes because its date appears somewhere in the document, ask the builder to verify bay, date and exact quote together on the cited line. Rerun all four fixed examples before trying another live draft.

premise: You are covering the help desk on a Saturday. Someone wants a quick status update and the name of the person in charge. You have a maintenance notice, so find how far that evidence takes you.
before: Notice A. Mail search maintenance, Saturday 09:00–09:30 UTC. Message delivery will continue.
try: In a fresh Copilot chat paste the notice. Ask for five rows: function, start, end, time zone and owner. Request the words from the notice that support each value. Then paste the same message as Notice B with “Owner: Taylor” added. Ask for the changed field only.
after: The first table says mail search, 09:00, 09:30, UTC and unspecified. The window is 30 minutes. In the second answer only the owner changes to Taylor. Delivery remains available in both notices.
why: A mail system has several jobs. Losing search access and losing the ability to receive a message would affect people differently. The notice identifies only one affected function.
rescue: If the answer gives the service desk as owner, ask “Which words in Notice A name the service desk?” When it cannot quote any, mark the field unspecified.

premise: A contractor offers a delivery day, and a colleague suggests another. You need to reply to the contractor without turning the suggestion into a booking. Think of each message as a separate piece of evidence.
before: M1 Approver: Tuesday is booked. M2 Organizer: Could we use Wednesday instead? M3 Approver: I will check.
try: Paste the three messages into Copilot. Ask for the last confirmed date, the proposed change and who owes the next response. Have it cite M1, M2 or M3 for each answer. Add a final message, “M4 Approver: Wednesday is now booked. Cancel Tuesday.” Ask the same questions again.
after: In the first view Tuesday is booked, Wednesday is proposed, and the approver is checking. After M4, Wednesday is booked, Tuesday is canceled, and this date question no longer needs a response.
why: A message can be newer than the confirmed decision without replacing it. The author’s words must actually accept the proposed change.
rescue: If its first draft says “Thanks for confirming Wednesday,” change the request to “Draft one sentence asking whether Wednesday is now confirmed.” Read the draft before treating it as correspondence.

premise: You have to explain a software fix to users and give the help desk a short note for handling questions. Both audiences should get identical instructions even though the two drafts sound different.
before: Build 12. A display bug affects iPad only. Fix rolls out Tuesday 14:00 UTC. Restart the app after rollout. Windows needs no action.
try: Paste the release note into Copilot Chat or the Copilot pane in Word. Request a 35-word user notice and three help-desk bullets. Read each draft once for time, once for platform and once for action. Replace the time sentence in the source with “Rollout time pending” and regenerate both drafts.
after: The first pair says affected iPad users restart after Tuesday 14:00 UTC and Windows users take no action. The revised drafts still give the iPad action but say that timing is pending. No 14:00 promise survives.
why: Writing less can remove the small words that carry the most meaning. Dropping “only” can send every user looking for an update.
rescue: If the help-desk version says all tablets are affected, request a revision quoting the platform from the source. Check the revised heading as well as the sentences underneath.

premise: You joined a meeting late. A Teams chat captures one suggestion and the available transcript captures a later decision. Your job is to record what actually happened without giving a job or deadline to the wrong person.
before: C1 09:03 Lee: Could exports run nightly? Transcript starts 09:10. T1 09:12 Kim: I approve weekly exports. T2 09:13 Lee: I will own the export job.
try: Paste the sample into work Copilot Chat. Ask for a row with decision, owner, deadline and evidence IDs, followed by open proposals. Make a second chat containing C1 and T2 only. Ask whether the shortened source establishes an approved frequency.
after: The full record supports weekly exports from T1 and Lee as owner from T2. No deadline appears. With T1 removed, the nightly proposal is visible, Lee still owns the job, and the approved schedule is unknown.
why: Someone accepting a job does not automatically accept every detail ever suggested for it. Separate the decision about frequency from the decision about ownership.
rescue: If nightly becomes approved in the second run, ask for the speaker and exact words of approval. The question mark in C1 is a clue that it was a proposal.

premise: A license sheet looks like a list of people until you notice that one person holds two plans and another assignment appears twice. You need the totals for rows, assignments and people. Each answers a different question.
before:
Row,Person,Plan
1,u1,A
2,u1,B
3,u2,A
4,u2,A
try: Paste the four rows and ask Copilot to list each distinct person-and-plan pair. Then ask it to make a second list of people alone. Finally append “5,,B”; tell it to count the physical row, flag its missing person, and exclude that row from identifiable assignments.
after: Initially there are four data rows, three distinct pairs (u1/A, u1/B, u2/A), and two people (u1, u2). The fifth row adds one physical row and one exception, while the identifiable pairs and people stay the same.
why: Counting rows is like counting tickets. One person can carry several tickets, and a copy of a ticket does not mean another person arrived.
rescue: If it reports three people after the last change, request the actual names on its list. Remove the blank entry from the distinct-person total while keeping its exception visible.

premise: You are preparing one slide about a pilot. The sponsor wants to know both how participating respondents felt and how much support is confirmed across the whole invitation list. A good slide makes both groups visible.
before: Pilot A: invited 12 sites; 9 replied; 6 respondents supported extension. No answers are available for the other 3 sites.
try: Put the counts in Copilot Chat or a Word brief you can reference in PowerPoint. Ask it to draft a headline, two labeled fractions and a speaker note. Divide 6 by 9 for the first audience and 6 by 12 for the second. Read the proposed headline aloud without looking at the notes.
after: Six of nine respondents supported extension, about 66.7%. Six of twelve invited sites gave recorded support, or 50%. A defensible headline is “Six sites endorsed the extension; three did not respond.”
why: A percentage always needs a group underneath it. The same six supporters form two thirds of the responding group and half of the invited group.
rescue: If the headline says two thirds of all sites supported continuation, ask it to show the denominator implied by “all.” Replace the headline itself; a footnote alone leaves the first impression wrong.

premise: You want the help desk to notice a queue just as it reaches the warning level. The test sheet deliberately includes numbers on both sides of the threshold and two bad entries, so you can see how the rule treats each.
before: Normal below 15 minutes; watch 15–29; investigate 30 and above; blank or negative invalid. A=14, B=15, C=29, D=30, E=blank, F=-1.
try: Give Copilot the rules and observations together. Ask for a row per letter and a total per status. Cover the answer and classify B and D yourself. Then change only A from 14 to 15 and ask for the revised counts.
after: At first A is normal, B and C are watch, D is investigate, and E and F are invalid. Counts are 1, 2, 1, 2. After the edit they are 0, 3, 1, 2.
why: Equality matters at a threshold. The rule deliberately includes 15 in watch and 30 in investigate. An empty observation provides no usable wait time.
rescue: If F is classified as normal, ask to see the order of the rules. Check for missing or negative values before testing “below 15.” Rerun F and A to verify the correction.

premise: Two versions of a move policy are on your desk. If you use the newest one automatically, a January request gets judged by a February rule. Make the assistant determine which rule was in force on the request date.
before: V1 from Jan 1 allows up to 20. V2 from Feb 1 allows up to 30; flagged groups held. A Jan 31 size 25; B Feb 1 size 30 clear; C Feb 2 size 12 flagged; D Feb 3 size 12 flag unknown.
try: Paste the four cases into Copilot and request a table of case, governing version, evidence and decision. Specify that groups above the active size limit are held. Next change only the V2 effective date to Feb 2 and rerun cases B and C.
after: Initially A is held, B allowed, C held and D unknown. Moving the effective date makes B subject to V1, so B is held. C still falls under V2 and remains held.
why: First choose the rule by date. Then apply its size limit and exceptions. A missing flag leaves a real gap when that flag can change the verdict.
rescue: If D gets allowed, ask “What would happen with the same size if its flag were true?” Since one possible answer is hold, ask it to request the missing flag.

premise: A help desk repeatedly answers questions about archive requests. Before asking people to rely on a handbook assistant, test it on a covered question, an unanswered question, and an incomplete question. Ordinary Copilot Chat works for this trial.
before: P1 Standard archive request: 5 business days. P2 Urgent archive request: 1 business day. Questions: Standard archive time? Restore time? Archive time?
try: Paste the two policy lines followed by the three questions. Tell Copilot to quote a clause for supported answers, say “not covered” when neither clause applies, and ask one question when the request type is missing. Edit P2 to 2 business days, start a fresh test and ask for the urgent time.
after: The first question gets 5 business days under P1. Restore is not covered. “Archive time?” needs a question about standard versus urgent. The revised source gives an urgent time of 2 business days.
why: Two services can have similar names and different promises. A careful assistant recognizes when a question uses a word the handbook never defines.
rescue: If it promises restoration in five days, ask it to highlight the word “restore” in P1. When it cannot, change that answer to “not covered.”

premise: An executive asks how many attempted moves finished successfully. Two batches are different sizes. A simple average of the displayed percentages gives the small batch as much say as the large one, which answers a different question.
before: West attempted 80 and completed 72. East attempted 20 and completed 10. Idle attempted 0 and completed 0.
try: Give Copilot the three batches. Ask for the numerator and denominator of each rate and the overall totals. Calculate the combined rate by adding the completed counts, then dividing by all attempts. Ask separately for the simple average of the two defined batch percentages. Finally change East to 22 completed out of 20.
after: West is 90% and East is 50%. The unweighted mean is 70%. Combined completion is 82 of 100, or 82%. Idle has no defined batch rate. The changed East record is invalid and should hold the summary for correction.
why: Imagine picking one attempted move at random. It is four times as likely to come from West as from East, so their percentages should not have equal influence in the combined result.
rescue: If Idle is shown as 0%, ask what completion rate zero attempts can demonstrate. Keep it out of the per-batch average.

premise: A mailbox storage report shows 30 GB before departments are added and 40 GB afterward. You have not received any new storage data. Trace which mailbox the department lookup counted twice.
before: Usage: m1=10 GB, m2=20 GB. Department map: m1→North, m1→South, m2→East.
try: Paste both lists into a fresh Copilot chat. Ask it to pair every usage row with every matching department and show the resulting rows before summing. Then ask for an exceptions table for IDs with multiple departments. Remove the South mapping and run the same calculation again.
after: The naive rows are North 10, South 10 and East 20. Their 40 GB sum includes the same 10 GB twice. The source total is 30 GB, with 10 GB initially ambiguous. After correction North has 10 and East has 20.
why: A lookup can return more than one answer. Matching m1 to two departments creates two report rows without creating another mailbox. The source total provides an independent check.
rescue: If the report splits m1 into five GB per department, ask where that allocation rule came from. Keep the 10 GB as an exception until the mapping is settled.

premise: Several log entries look like they happened on different days. Before telling an incident team which event came first, put every observation onto the same clock and set aside anything without enough time information.
before: A Jan 5 23:55 -0600 delay; B Jan 6 06:02 +0000 peak; C Jan 6 01:10 -0500 recovery; D 00:59 configuration note, date and offset unknown.
try: Paste these records into Copilot and request an ordered UTC table that retains the letters. For A, add six hours yourself and check the resulting date. Ask for elapsed time from A to C. Add Jan 6 and -0500 to D, rerun, and ask what that timing proves about the cause.
after: The known events are A at 05:55Z, B at 06:02Z and C at 06:10Z on Jan 6. Fifteen minutes elapsed from first observation to recovery. D, initially unplaceable, later fits at 05:59Z, four minutes after A.
why: A UTC offset tells you how far the local clock differs from the reference clock. Item order can be verified from time alone. A causal explanation needs additional evidence.
rescue: If it places D before A initially, ask which date and offset it assumed. Move D into an unknown-time row until both are supplied.

premise: The release checklist needs three independent items. One has a time limit and another is still pending. Evaluate the same packet one minute apart so you can see exactly when an otherwise good backup becomes too old.
before: Gate requires approved rollback, successful backup no more than 60 minutes old, and every smoke test passed. R1 approved rollback. B1 successful backup 09:00 UTC. T1 two passed, one pending.
try: Ask Copilot for three evidence rows at 10:00 and again at 10:01 the same day. Have it calculate backup age and give an overall verdict only after filling in all three rows. Change T1 to “three passed” and repeat both checks.
after: Initially both times hold because testing is incomplete. At 10:00 the backup is exactly 60 minutes old and qualifies. At 10:01 its age is 61 minutes. With all tests passed, only 10:00 gives GO; 10:01 still gives HOLD.
why: Think of the gate as three switches wired together. Turning the testing switch on helps only while every other switch also passes.
rescue: If it allows the 10:01 release, ask for the subtraction “10:01 minus 09:00” in minutes and compare 61 with the stated limit.

premise: A user clicks Submit twice. Your practice agent should show which ticket it would file and which submission it would reuse. Run this entirely on a paper ledger inside chat so you can inspect each decision.
before: R1 | project alpha; R1 | project alpha; R2 | project beta; R1 | project gamma. The first field is the request ID.
try: Give Copilot an empty ledger and the requests in this exact order. Ask it to create a row for a new ID, return the existing row for an identical repeat, and flag changed content under an existing ID. Request a snapshot after the third event, then append R3 | project alpha.
after: The first four outcomes are create, reuse, create and conflict. After event three the ledger has R1=alpha and R2=beta. The conflict preserves R1=alpha. R3 adds a third row, even though its text matches alpha.
why: The ID identifies the request; its description describes it. The same description can belong to two genuine requests. A repeat delivery can also carry a conflicting description.
rescue: If R1 changes to gamma, ask the assistant to replay only event four against the saved snapshot and display the conflict separately from the stored row.

premise: A sponsor wants to release a rollout because the completion chart looks good. Your job is to check whether the owner also approved. Build the decision memo and slide from the same evidence so they cannot quietly contradict each other.
before: G1: at least 95% completed AND owner approval. R1 North 48/50. R2 South 47/50. M1 owner: I can review tomorrow. M2 participant: We should move ahead.
try: Paste the packet and ask Copilot for a one-paragraph memo, a headline and one evidence row per requirement. Add M3 “owner: I approve release” and request the new verdict. Finally edit R2 to 46/50 and run it once more.
after: At first 95 of 100 completed, but approval is pending, so HOLD. M3 gives GO with the same 95%. The revised South count lowers the total to 94%, bringing back HOLD even with the owner’s approval.
why: A decision requiring two conditions can fail for two different reasons. Keeping each condition visible explains why the verdict changes while some evidence remains valid.
rescue: If the first headline says “Ready to release,” ask for the owner’s exact approval words. Revise the headline itself to identify the pending sign-off.

premise: Imagine two mail routes, one for everyday items and one for large items. The team disagrees about an item exactly 25 MB in size. You can answer that by reading one comparison in a tiny local file.
before: In route.py: def route(size_mb): return "large" if size_mb >= 25 else "normal". The four example sizes are 0, 24, 25 and 26 MB.
try: Open Claude Code in a practice folder and save the given function in route.py. Ask it to read the file and predict the four labels without editing it. Write down what you think happens to 25. In your editor change >= to >, save the file, and ask Claude to read it again.
after: Originally you get normal, normal, large, large. After that one-character change the labels are normal, normal, normal, large. Only the exactly-25 case switches.
why: The equals part lets an item sitting precisely on the cutoff into the large group. Removing it leaves only items beyond the cutoff in that group.
rescue: If the second answer still says large at 25, reopen the saved file, inspect its comparison, and ask Claude to quote the current line before it predicts again.

premise: A new teammate needs to know which shared resources still lack owners. A blank cell is a useful exception to report. Let Claude Code turn a four-row inventory into a short, checkable handoff.
before: owners.csv contains name,owner on the first line, then Shipping,Ari; Facilities,; Design Lab,Kim; Front Desk,. Put each pair on its own line.
try: Open your practice folder in Claude Code and ask it to read owners.csv and create handoff.md. Request total resources, number with owners and the exact names missing owners. Open the new note yourself. Now fill the Facilities owner with Lee, save the CSV and have Claude rebuild the same note.
after: The first handoff says four resources, two owned, with Facilities and Front Desk unassigned. After the update it still says four resources, three owned, and only Front Desk missing an owner.
why: The resource name is present even when its owner is blank. Dropping that entire row would make the summary look cleaner while hiding the very work the teammate needs to do.
rescue: If it lists “Front” and “Desk” separately, ask it to parse by comma and preserve spaces within a name. Recheck the total against the four data lines.

premise: A release-note style should survive a fresh conversation. Store the formatting rule in the project so you can give the next session new facts without teaching the heading order again.
before: CLAUDE.md says: use exactly “## Change” then “## Verification,” each with one plain sentence. Release 1.2 fixes a duplicate reminder and was checked on two devices.
try: In the practice folder, create CLAUDE.md with that rule. Ask Claude Code to write release.md for version 1.2. Inspect the headings and facts. Start a fresh Claude Code session in that same folder. Request release-next.md for a corrected date label checked on one device, without restating the style.
after: Both files contain the two required headings in the same order. The first note mentions the duplicate reminder and two devices. The second mentions the date label and one device, with no reference to the old reminder problem.
why: The project file carries the writing convention. The facts come from the current assignment. Separating those lets the form stay stable while the content changes.
rescue: If the new note has a Summary heading, check the folder and exact name CLAUDE.md in both sessions. Then ask Claude to reread it and regenerate only release-next.md.

premise: An address list contains accidental spaces, upper-case letters and repeat entries. People expect the original order to survive cleanup. That last requirement matters even when the final number of addresses is correct.
before: A practice list is [" Z@X ", "a@x", "z@x", " "]. The rule trims outer spaces, lowercases letters, skips blanks and keeps only the first appearance.
try: Prepare cases.tsv from the lab fixture. Ask Claude Code to create unique_addresses(values) in addresses.py and run the sample tests. Then give it the four-value practice list from this example. Ask it to show each original string beside its cleaned value before displaying the final list.
after: The cleaned sequence is z@x, a@x, z@x, then an empty string. The final output is ["z@x","a@x"]. An empty input list gives []. Neither answer should contain a blank address.
why: Keep the first item as it arrives. Checking whether you have already seen an address helps drop later copies; sorting the final items would throw away the arrival order.
rescue: If the output starts with a@x, request removal of any final sorting step. Rerun this order-sensitive case and both TSV checks.

premise: You are about to change a mailbox warning rule. First agree what the rule means and how to test it; otherwise a passing test might only confirm that the code and its author made the same assumption.
before: thresholds.txt: A mailbox warns at 90 percent inclusive. Below 90 is OK. A missing percentage is UNKNOWN. The practice inputs are 89, 90 and None.
try: Save thresholds.txt in a practice folder. In Claude Code’s Plan mode, request the three inputs, expected outputs and reasoning without writing any files. Compare 90 with the word “inclusive.” When the plan matches, switch to a mode that permits edits and ask for classify(value) in quota.py plus its three tests.
after: Planning produces a test table before the implementation changes. Once implemented and run, 89 returns OK, 90 returns WARNING, and None returns UNKNOWN. The missing-value test completes without a crash.
why: A missing reading has no numerical size. It deserves its own question before asking whether it crossed a threshold. Defining that case first prevents a surprise during implementation.
rescue: If Claude describes code but quota.py never appears, check whether the session is still in Plan mode. If None crashes, ask it to handle missing input before making a numerical comparison.

premise: An inventory report lists only groups whose owner field has text. The missing line makes it look as though an entire group disappeared. Reproduce the fault before asking for a fix so you can tell exactly what changed.
before: groups.py holds [("Ops","Kai"),("HR",""),("Docs","Lou")]. A loop prints name and owner only inside the condition if owner.
try: Run the original file in your scratch folder and keep the printed output. Ask Claude Code to show every group once, preserve its input order and label each blank owner UNASSIGNED. Have it run again. Append ("Lab","") to the input and ask for a third run.
after: Originally only Ops Kai and Docs Lou print. After the final edit the four lines read Ops Kai, HR UNASSIGNED, Docs Lou and Lab UNASSIGNED. The two missing owner fields are now visible.
why: The conditional used to control whether the whole row appeared. The desired report always prints the row; only the displayed owner label depends on whether there is a value.
rescue: If Lab fails to appear, ask Claude to show the loop with its indentation intact. Move the print operation outside any condition that filters blank owners, then rerun all four rows.

premise: You write the same type of release note every week. A project skill lets you call a saved recipe by name; its instructions should read the latest facts each time rather than repeating last week’s evidence.
before: changes.txt initially contains “Change: export now keeps empty departments.” and “Evidence: 4 fixture rows passed.” A fixture row is one made-up example used for testing.
try: Ask Claude Code to create .claude/skills/note/SKILL.md in the practice project. Give the skill the name note and directions to read changes.txt, write note.md, and use exactly the headings Change and Evidence. Open a new session in that folder. Enter /note, inspect the result, change 4 to 6 in changes.txt, save and invoke /note again.
after: The second note keeps the two headings, describes the same export change, and reports six fixture rows passed. Open note.md itself to check it was rewritten.
why: The recipe lives in one file. The ingredients live in another. A useful recipe deliberately reads its ingredients each time it runs.
rescue: If /note never appears, inspect the full folder path, the capitalization of SKILL.md and the skill name. Reopen the session in the project containing that file.

premise: You have a current group list and a desired group list. You want a preview of what would change before anyone changes access. The job uses a local JSON file and prints a proposal you can check by hand.
before: members.json contains {"current":[" Ari ","BO","bo","Cy"],"desired":["ari","Dee","","DEE"]}. Treat letter case and outer spaces as insignificant and skip blanks.
try: Save the JSON in the practice folder. Ask Claude Code to produce preview.py and print three sorted arrays called add, remove and keep. Compare the two cleaned lists yourself. For a second run, copy the entire current array into desired so both input lists are identical.
after: The first preview adds dee, removes bo and cy, and keeps ari. In the second preview add and remove are empty and keep contains ari, bo and cy. Neither run changes any real membership.
why: The clean current list has three distinct names; “BO” and “bo” describe the same one. Comparing the raw spellings would create changes that do not exist under the stated rule.
rescue: If ari appears under both add and remove, inspect how each side was cleaned. Ask Claude to print the normalized lists before calculating their differences.

premise: A single word in a guest-sharing policy changed. Instead of guessing its impact from the version number, turn the two rules into a small table and identify precisely who sees different behavior.
before: V1 allows members. Guests are allowed when days < 7, otherwise reviewed. V2 still allows members. Guests are allowed when days <= 7, otherwise reviewed.
try: Save both rules as policies.txt. Ask Claude Code to implement decide(version, kind, days) in your practice folder, then print V1 and V2 side by side for guests and members on days 7 and 8. Compare rows before looking at its prose explanation. Count the rows with changed outcomes.
after: A guest on day 7 changes from REVIEW to ALLOW. A guest on day 8 remains REVIEW. A member is ALLOW on both days under both editions. Exactly one of the four comparisons differs.
why: Adding equality extends the guest exception by one day. Members take a different branch of the rule, so the guest cutoff should never change their result.
rescue: If members on day 8 are under review, ask Claude to evaluate the member rule before examining the guest cutoff. Then rerun all four comparisons.

premise: A service returns a list in pages. An empty middle page still has directions to another page. If your report stops just because it saw no items, it will quietly lose the final record. Rehearse this entirely with local files.
before: pages.json describes one: items M1,M2 → two; two: no items → three; three: items M2,M3 → null (end).
try: Use the lab’s JSON fixture. Ask Claude Code to make paged.py start at one, follow each next value and preserve only the first occurrence of each item. Request the sequence of page names it visited. Then make three point back to one, run again, and finally point three to an absent page.
after: The good chain visits one, two, three and returns ["M1","M2","M3"]. M2 appears once. The loop produces a repeated-page error; the broken link produces a missing-page error. Neither malformed chain should report a partial list as a successful result.
why: The next pointer tells the reader whether the journey continues. An empty page describes only the contents of that stop.
rescue: If M3 disappears, find the condition that stops the loop. It should stop on the end marker, while still checking for missing or previously visited pages.

premise: A test sometimes passes and sometimes fails because it asks the computer what time it is right now. Freeze the reference time so the same input always gives the same answer, including the exact instant a deadline arrives.
before: expiry.csv: A deadline 2026-12-31 23:59:59Z; B deadline 2027-01-01 00:00:00Z; C deadline 2027-01-01 00:00:01Z. Z means UTC.
try: Enter the three rows from the lab fixture. Ask Claude Code for a classifier that accepts an explicit as_of time and expires an item when that time is equal to or later than its deadline. Run at midnight Jan 1 UTC twice, then at one second past midnight. Ask for IDs as well as counts.
after: At midnight A and B have expired, and C is still active. Both midnight runs agree. At 00:00:01Z all three have expired.
why: An appointment can be over exactly when its deadline arrives. The choice to include equality is deliberate, and the one-second cases expose code that rounds time to whole minutes.
rescue: If B stays active, inspect whether the comparison uses > rather than >=. If C expires early, check that the parser and test data preserve the seconds field.

premise: A program imports events into a small local database. Suppose it stops halfway through. You need to resume without counting old events again or letting a duplicate overwrite an amount the system already accepted.
before: events.csv contains E1,4; E2,8; E1,4; E3,5 under the headers id,amount. Use a disposable SQLite database in the practice folder.
try: Ask Claude Code to build the importer with one saved transaction per input row and event ID as the unique key. Trigger its practice stop after two rows. Inspect the database, then rerun the original input twice against the same database. Append E2,99 to the CSV and run one more time.
after: Immediately after the stop, E1 and E2 total 12. After retry the three IDs E1, E2 and E3 total 17. The final conflicting repeat leaves E2 at 8 and the total at 17.
why: The ID is the receipt showing the event already arrived. An interruption after two saved rows should not erase those receipts or make them new events on retry.
rescue: If the total rises to 108 after the conflict, ask whether an existing E2 was replaced with 99. Implement the stated first-value rule, reset the scratch database and replay the full sequence.

premise: You are changing the shape of an address field so a new tool can read its two parts. A successful conversion should let you travel there and back without losing any original value, including a deliberately missing address.
before: Three people have addresses a@example.org, null and b@c@example.org. Their notes are “A, B”, an empty string and “x”. Keep their IDs 1, 2 and 3 in order.
try: Start from the exact people.json in the lab. Ask Claude Code to write forward.py, splitting each address at its last @ into a local part and a domain, and reverse.py, rebuilding roundtrip.json. Request a comparison of the parsed original and rebuilt records. Leave people.json untouched.
after: The third address splits into b@c and example.org and comes back as b@c@example.org. The second address stays a JSON null, its note remains an empty string, and all three records return in the original order.
why: Looking at the printed files can be misleading. Indentation can change harmlessly, while turning an absent address into the four letters “null” would change its meaning.
rescue: If round-trip equality fails, print the first differing ID, field, value and value type. Fix the transformation for that case and rerun both directions.

premise: Two systems recorded the same incident with different clock offsets. Some rows report the same event twice; two disagree about its state. Build a timeline that keeps the contradiction visible instead of selecting a winner by accident.
before: R1 at 01:20 -05:00 queued; R2 at 01:05 -06:00 done; R1 at 06:20Z queued; R2 at 07:05Z failed. All dates are November 1, 2026.
try: Save observations.csv exactly as in the lab, including its header. Ask Claude Code to convert all times to UTC, sort by instant, group by event ID, and list source row numbers for conflicting states. Change the last state from failed to done and rebuild incident.md.
after: The two R1 records agree at 06:20Z. R2 comes later at 07:05Z and initially conflicts on source rows 3 and 5 when the header is row 1. After the edit there are still two distinct IDs and zero state conflicts.
why: The smallest local clock reading is not necessarily the earliest event. Normalizing the clocks first and checking all observations for each ID answers two separate questions.
rescue: If the first report shows no conflict, ask whether it discarded repeat IDs before comparing their states. Preserve both source rows until the comparison is complete.

premise: A candidate pricing change looks reasonable at a glance. A reviewer needs evidence that it implements the promised two free items and charges consistently once the free allowance is exhausted. Work with a local copy and write the expected amounts before running the candidate.
before: Contract: first two items free; each further item costs $1.25; counts are nonnegative whole numbers. Candidate subtracts one free item: max(0,n-1)*1.25.
try: Put the contract in release.txt and ask Claude Code to write independent expected values for -1, 0, 2, 3 and 6. Run the candidate in fee.py and record the initial failure in evidence.md. Only then request the fix. Use the reviewer command in evidence.md to rerun from the scratch folder.
after: The original candidate incorrectly charges $1.25 at two items. After repair, negative input is rejected, 0 and 2 display 0.00, 3 displays 1.25, and 6 displays 5.00. The documented reviewer command reproduces these results.
why: Two of six items are free, leaving four billable items. Four times $1.25 is $5.00. This arithmetic gives the reviewer an answer independent of the code.
rescue: If six still displays 6.25, inspect whether the program subtracts just one free item. Change the implementation and retain the independent expected amounts when running the tests again.

premise: You are leaving a shift and someone asks whether both practice messages were delivered. The file records several moments in each message’s journey. Your job is to report the last thing actually observed for each message.
before: trace.log has four lines in order: A queued, B queued, A retrying, A delivered. It has no header, so “A queued” counts as line 1.
try: Open the project folder in Codex, paste the lab prompt and ask it to show the final row for each ID with its line number. Then append B delivered to the file as line 5, save and ask for just the changed row.
after: Before your edit the evidence is A delivered on line 4 and B queued on line 2. Afterward, B becomes delivered on line 5. The evidence for A stays on line 4.
why: A later line updates only the ID printed on that line. A queue entry alone cannot tell you whether the delivery eventually failed.
rescue: If the answer calls B stuck or failed, ask “Show me the line that records failure.” Have Codex use the observed word queued until a later line supports a newer state.

premise: You want a two-screen handoff on a laptop. Someone should be able to open it, move forward once, then return to the start without accidentally landing on an empty page.
before: Create pages.txt with Check queue on the first line and Verify delivery on the second. The normal newline at the end of the file is fine.
try: Ask Codex to create the single index.html described in the lab. Double-click that file in Finder or File Explorer. Before clicking, read the title, the counter and the Previous button. Click Next once, try the same button again, then click Previous.
after: The first screen shows Check queue and 1 of 2, with Previous disabled. The second shows Verify delivery and 2 of 2, with Next disabled. Previous returns to Check queue and 1 of 2.
why: The counter makes a hidden error visible. An apparently harmless extra blank line in a text file can become a third page if the program treats it as a title.
rescue: If you see 1 of 3, ask Codex to ignore trailing blank titles, rebuild the same HTML file and reload it. Repeat all three clicks on the saved page.

premise: Two players have finished a few practice rounds. One lost points and another played a zero-point round. You need to preserve both facts when preparing the scoreboard.
before: The ledger contains Ari 80, Bea 35, Ari -75, Bea 0, and Ari 10, in that order. After the first check you will add Bea -40.
try: Save the rows in ledger.csv with the lab’s player,points header. Ask Codex to build and run totals.py. Read each player’s round count as well as the points. Append Bea,-40, save and ask Codex to run exactly the same script again.
after: Ari has three rounds and 15 points because 80 − 75 + 10 = 15. Bea begins with two rounds and 35 points. Her third round changes the total to −5. Ari’s line stays first.
why: A zero contributes nothing to points but still represents a round. A negative entry subtracts from what the player already has. Counting rows and adding points answer different questions.
rescue: If Bea shows one round on the first run, ask to see where the script skips entries. Keep numeric zero as a valid score and rerun the original five rows.

premise: A teammate needs every findings file to have the same shape. You want the convention to apply even when you start a new conversation with no reminder in the message.
before: AGENTS.md says a findings file is an array of objects with only id and status, uppercase statuses, sorted by ascending ID. Your first two facts are A1 open and A2 closed.
try: Open the folder containing AGENTS.md in Codex. Paste the lab prompt and open the generated findings.json. Start a fresh project chat, staying in this folder, and request second-findings.json for Z9 closed and B2 open. Give only the facts.
after: The first file contains A1 OPEN and A2 CLOSED. The second contains B2 OPEN before Z9 CLOSED, even though Z9 appeared first in the request. Each object has exactly two keys.
why: The project instructions live on disk and can be picked up by a fresh chat. Using a second pair of facts tests whether the rule travels without copying the old content.
rescue: If the second file has lowercase statuses, check the active directory and exact filename AGENTS.md. Reopen the project from that folder and repeat with the same second pair.

premise: Two exports overlap because an earlier snapshot arrived late. A human reader can see that revision 2 replaces revision 1, even though the row for revision 1 appears later. Your importer needs the same judgment.
before: versions.csv contains x,2,New; y,1,First; x,1,Old; y,1,First, with one record per line below the header. The y entries are exact repeats.
try: Run the lab prompt, let Codex create merge.py, and open merged.csv. Save a copy of this successful output. Append x,2,Conflict to the input, save and rerun. Compare the current output with your saved copy.
after: The successful merge contains x,2,New and y,1,First in ID order. The later run reports conflicting labels for x at revision 2, and the previously saved output is byte-for-byte identical.
why: A higher revision chooses the newer record. Two different labels claiming the same ID and revision leave no reliable winner. The previous successful report remains useful while someone investigates.
rescue: If an empty merged.csv replaces your good one after the conflict, ask Codex when it opens the destination. Have it validate the entire input first, recreate the valid report and repeat the failure test.

premise: Imagine searching a mini index on a small screen. A reader types a few letters, sees no match, then clears the field. The list should always explain what happened.
before: titles.txt contains four lines: Mailbox Review, Group Audit, Mail Flow, Archive Plan. The first and third titles both contain mail.
try: Ask Codex to build the single HTML file, open it in your browser and write down the initial count. Search for mail, then put a space on each side and switch the letters to uppercase. Replace the query with xyz and finally clear the field.
after: Both mail searches return Mailbox Review followed by Mail Flow, with a count of 2. The xyz search shows 0 and an explicit empty message. Clearing the query restores all four titles in the original order.
why: A good search cleans the reader’s query before matching it. Clearing a query is another input change, so the page needs to redraw the complete list.
rescue: If four entries never come back, ask Codex what happens when the cleaned query is an empty string. Request a test for clearing the field after a zero-result search, then reload the updated page.

premise: A change looks tiny during code review. Someone replaced a comparison operator. Your job is to show whether a real user could get a different result at the exact limit.
before: The committed cap.py says return count <= 5. A saved but uncommitted edit changes the line to return count < 5. All inputs in this exercise are nonnegative whole numbers.
try: Create the Git baseline and edit as directed in the lab. Ask Codex to inspect the uncommitted diff without changing it. Give it 4, 5 and 6 as sample inputs and request the old and new results side by side.
after: For 4, both versions return True. For 5, the committed rule returns True and the edited rule returns False. For 6, both return False. Restoring the equals sign gives True, True, False again.
why: Both expressions allow counts below five and reject counts above it. The equals sign controls the single value exactly on the boundary. That value is the simplest way to demonstrate the change.
rescue: If Codex finds no difference, run git diff in this practice folder. Save the edited file and confirm you committed the <= version before comparing the two.

premise: You want the answer from one Codex run to be readable by another program. You will compare the shape of the saved answer against the task’s actual counts.
before: The first sample is sent, held, sent, unknown. counts.schema.json declares three required integer fields called sent, held and unknown, and disallows additional fields.
try: In the practice folder run the complete codex exec command from the lab, including --output-schema counts.schema.json and -o result.json. Open result.json itself. Repeat the command with only held, held as the sample and direct the output to second.json.
after: The first answer has sent 2, held 1 and unknown 1. The second has sent 0, held 2 and unknown 0. The field order can differ. Both files contain exactly the three named fields and ordinary integers.
why: A schema enforces an answer’s structure. It cannot guarantee that four actual events were counted correctly. Adding the three values checks that the first total equals four and the second equals two.
rescue: If you see progress text alongside the JSON, check the file written by -o rather than copying the whole terminal transcript. If the counts differ, ask for the four input labels in order and recount.

premise: A manager wants counts to share outside the team. The source includes addresses and individual notes, but neither belongs in the final report. You will inspect the saved file as a reader would receive it.
before: The three fictional records have statuses OK, blank and ok. Every row has an example.invalid address and a message. Blank status means unknown.
